rationale: The book's cited texts define righteousness performatively and do so explicitly: Deuteronomy 6:25 states outright that observing to do all the commandments 'shall be our righteousness'; Psalm 119:172 equates the commandments themselves with righteousness; and 1 John 3:7 — framed as a warning against deception on precisely this point — says the one who DOES righteousness is righteous. The proving chapter then anchors the garment elaboration in the Greek of Revelation 19:8 (dikaiomata, plural 'righteous acts', so rendered by ASV/ESV/NASB/NIV against the KJV's flattened 'righteousness of saints'), and corroborates it with Job 29:14, Isaiah 61:10, Zechariah 3:4, Revelation 3:4, 16:15, and 22:14. Crucially, the book pre-empts the two strongest counter-texts: it explains Isaiah 64:6 (the rag is stained by the doer's iniquity, not by the deed's nature — the same verse names the iniquities) and it retains the grace-source of the garment ('it was given unto her'; Ephesians 2:10), so it is not a works-wage doctrine. The forensic-imputation counter-reading, by contrast, must read Deuteronomy 6:25 against its plain positive grammar (as an unattainable standard), must flatten the plural dikaiomata of Revelation 19:8 into a status, and leaves the wedding-garment expulsion, 'keep thy garments', and 'they that do his commandments' (Rev 22:14) without a mechanism. Under the accepted prior premises (faith = faithfulness, belief = obedient response, love = commandment-keeping), even Genesis 15:6 coheres with the book's reading. The book explains all supplied evidence; the counter explains a subset and strains the rest.
book_core_identification: Righteousness in Scripture is the doing of God's commandments — righteous acts actually performed (the law observed and kept) — not a vague moral goodness and not merely a legal verdict or status received apart from doing.
book_secondary_elaborations: Righteous acts are pictured as a garment: the fine linen of Revelation 19:8 (dikaiomata) is the law kept and worn, the covenant worn as the name is the covenant owned.
The garment is granted by God ('it was given unto her'; Eph 2:10) yet must be put on, kept clean, and worn by the saint — given, then worn.
Nakedness is the counter-symbol: absence of righteous acts, covenant exposure (the speechless wedding guest, Laodicea, Rev 16:15).
Filthy rags (Isa 64:6) describe deeds stained by the doer's iniquity, not obedience as intrinsically filthy; the remedy is washing (Isa 1:16-18; Rev 7:14; Zech 3:4), not disrobing.
The armor of God (Eph 6:14; Isa 59:17) is God's own clothing of righteousness lent to the wearer; baptism is the once-for-all bath, foot-washing the daily cleansing of the walk.
strongest_counter_interpretation: The classic Protestant forensic reading: righteousness is fundamentally a legal standing before God — Christ's righteousness credited (imputed) to the believer through faith apart from works (Gen 15:6; Rom 3:21-26; 4:3-8; 2 Cor 5:21; Phil 3:9). On this reading, texts like Deuteronomy 6:25 state the law's standard that fallen humanity cannot meet (thus driving the sinner to imputed righteousness), obedience texts describe the fruit of justification rather than righteousness itself, and the white garment imagery pictures the imputed covering, with Isaiah 64:6 proving that human righteous deeds are worthless as a covering.
counter_core_identification: Righteousness is primarily a forensic status — a right standing before God declared and credited to the believer on the basis of Christ's righteousness received by faith, explicitly apart from works of obedience.
material_core_denial: The counter denies that righteousness IS the doing of the commandments; it asserts that righteousness is a verdict received apart from works, so that Deuteronomy 6:25, Psalm 119:172, and 1 John 3:7 describe either an unattainable legal standard or the downstream fruit of a righteousness already possessed by imputation — the two identifications cannot both be the primary referent of the same term.
counter_case: Romans 4:3-8: righteousness is 'counted' to the one who 'worketh not' but believes — apparently defining righteousness as credited apart from doing.
Philippians 3:9: Paul renounces 'mine own righteousness, which is of the law' for 'the righteousness which is of God by faith'.
2 Corinthians 5:21: believers 'become the righteousness of God in him' — a conferred identity, not performed acts.
Isaiah 64:6: 'all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags' — human righteous deeds cannot constitute the covering.
Genesis 15:6: Abraham's belief, not his commandment-keeping, is counted as righteousness.
The garment imagery (Isa 61:10; Zech 3:4) shows righteousness bestowed by God on the unworthy, consistent with imputation.
book_explanatory_advantages: Deuteronomy 6:25 is an explicit definitional statement in the book's favor: doing the commandments 'shall be our righteousness' — the forensic reading must invert its plain positive sense into a counterfactual standard.
Psalm 119:172 flatly equates commandments with righteousness, requiring no mediation.
1 John 3:7 is framed as an anti-deception warning that doing righteousness is what makes one righteous — a verse that directly targets the 'status without deeds' reading the book opposes.

Revelation 19:8's Greek dikaiomata is plural and active ('righteous acts of the saints', per ASV/ESV/NASB/NIV); the book explains why the wedding garment is made of deeds, why the guest without it is expelled, and why saints must 'keep their garments' (Rev 3:4; 16:15) — mechanics the pure-status reading cannot supply, since an imputed status cannot be defiled by conduct or kept by watching.

The book absorbs the counter's best proof-texts: Isaiah 64:6 is read in its own context (the doers' iniquities stain the deeds), and the grace objection is answered by Revelation 19:8's own first clause ('it was given unto her') plus Ephesians 2:10 — deeds ordained and granted by God, then walked in.
Job 29:14, Isaiah 59:17/Ephesians 6:14, and Isaiah 61:10 form a cross-Testament garment pattern where righteousness is uniformly something put on and worn as conduct.

Accepted prior premises (faith = faithfulness/obedience; belief = obedient response; love = commandment-keeping) make Genesis 15:6 and the Pauline faith-righteousness texts cohere with performed righteousness rather than against it.
Revelation 22:14 blesses 'they that do his commandments, that they may have right to the tree of life' — the terminal beatitude matches the book's definition exactly.
counter_explanatory_advantages: Romans 4:4-5's 'to him that worketh not' is more naturally read on the forensic account and is not directly exegeted in the supplied chapter.
Philippians 3:9's explicit contrast between 'mine own righteousness of the law' and righteousness 'through faith' sits more comfortably with a received-status reading.

The forensic reading gives a simpler account of how the ungodly sinner is first accepted before any track record of obedience exists (the prodigal robed 'before the boy can finish his speech' — a detail the book itself concedes).
decisive_sources: Deuteronomy 6:25 — an explicit scriptural definition: doing the commandments 'shall be our righteousness'
1 John 3:7 — 'he that doeth righteousness is righteous', framed as a warning against the contrary teaching
Revelation 19:8 — dikaiomata, 'the righteous acts of the saints', as the fine linen, with the 'was given' clause answering the grace objection
Isaiah 64:6 read in context — the deeds are stained by the named iniquities, defusing the strongest counter-text
Revelation 3:4; 16:15; 22:14 — garments defiled, kept, and commandments done, mechanics only a performative reading supplies
Prior accepted findings: faith = faithfulness, belief = obedient response, love = commandment-keeping, which harmonize Genesis 15:6 and faith-righteousness texts with the book's core
unresolved_objections: Romans 4:4-8 ('to him that worketh not... his faith is counted for righteousness') and Philippians 3:9 are not directly exegeted in the supplied bundle; the book relies on the prior faith-as-faithfulness premise to harmonize them rather than treating them head-on.

The initial-acceptance question — how the repentant sinner with no accumulated righteous acts is first clothed (the prodigal's robe, Zechariah 3:4's exchange of raiment) — is acknowledged but shows that a granted covering precedes the wearer's performance, a sequencing the entry's polemical phrasing ('not a verdict only received') compresses.
The book does not adjudicate 2 Corinthians 5:21's 'become the righteousness of God in him', which the imputation reading claims as its clearest text.
